title: Linked lists: nodes, traversal, insertion and deletion
learningObjectives: Describe a singly linked list as nodes containing a data value and a pointer to the next node.
Explain the roles of the head pointer, NULL terminator and pointer-to-pointer parameters.
Traverse a list safely and identify the O(n) cost of searching for a value.
Insert nodes at the front and delete a matching node while preserving the remaining links.
Use malloc and free with checked allocation, explicit ownership and complete cleanup.
Test empty, one-node, head, middle, tail, missing-value and allocation-failure cases.

understand.concept: A singly linked list is a sequence of separately stored nodes. Each node contains a data value and a pointer to the next node. The head pointer identifies the first node; the final node points to NULL. Unlike an array, list elements do not need to occupy adjacent memory locations.
understand.whyItMatters: Linked lists allow insertion or removal near a known node without shifting later elements. They help learners understand pointer relationships and dynamic memory ownership. Every allocated node must eventually be freed.
understand.analogy: Think of a chain of cards: each card stores information and an arrow to the next card. The head is the first card, and the final arrow points to nothing.
understand.analogyLimit: Real C pointers are addresses, not safe visual arrows. A wrong pointer update can lose the rest of the list, create a cycle or access freed memory. The analogy also does not show allocation failure.

explain.narrative:
A node can be declared as `struct Node { int value; struct Node *next; };`. The list is represented by a pointer to its first node. An empty list has head == NULL. To traverse, start at head and follow next until the current pointer becomes NULL. Never dereference a NULL pointer.

To insert at the front, allocate a node, check that malloc did not return NULL, initialize its value and next pointer, then update the caller's head. A function that changes the caller's head can receive `struct Node **head`. For deletion, keep a pointer to the link that points to the current node. When the target is found, redirect that link to current->next before freeing current. This handles deletion of the head and a later node using the same logic.

The example uses a clear ownership rule: the list owns every node successfully allocated for it, and the caller must eventually destroy the list. Do not use a node after free, free the same node twice, or lose the only pointer to an allocated node. Front insertion is O(1); traversal and search are O(n); deleting a value after searching is O(n).

examples.title: Insert, traverse, delete and free a singly linked list
examples.explanation: push_front allocates and initializes a node before publishing it as the new head. remove_first uses a pointer to the link that owns the current node, so removing the first node and a later node follow the same pointer-update pattern. It reconnects the list before freeing the removed node. destroy_list saves the next pointer before freeing each current node, then clears the caller's head.

examples.title: Traverse a list without modifying it
examples.explanation: The nodes have automatic storage duration and are linked in reverse declaration order. The traversal receives a pointer to const node and only reads values and next pointers. It stops at NULL and does not allocate or free these nodes.

practise.guidedTask: Draw three nodes containing 10, 20 and 30. Trace head and every next pointer while inserting 5 at the front, deleting 20, deleting the head value 5, and searching for 99. After each operation identify which nodes remain reachable from head.
practise.independentTask: Extend the list with append, contains and remove_all operations. Define whether duplicates are allowed, check allocation failures and write a destroy function. Test empty lists, one node, deleting head/middle/tail, missing values and cleanup after partial construction.
hints: An empty singly linked list is represented by head == NULL.
Allocate and initialize a new node before changing existing list links.
A pointer-to-pointer can represent the link that points to the current node, including the head link.
Save the next pointer before freeing a node during cleanup.
After unlinking a node, never read its fields; free it exactly once.
Document ownership: every successfully allocated node must remain reachable until it is freed.

questions.prompt: What marks the end of a conventional singly linked list?
options: A next pointer equal to NULL
A node with value zero
The largest data value
The head pointer becoming an integer
questions.answer: A next pointer equal to NULL
questions.explanation: The final node's next pointer is NULL, so traversal knows there is no following node.

questions.prompt: Why does push_front receive struct Node **head?
options: So it can update the caller's head pointer
So every node becomes constant
So malloc cannot fail
So the list is automatically sorted
questions.answer: So it can update the caller's head pointer
questions.explanation: The function needs to modify the pointer variable owned by the caller, so it receives that variable's address.

questions.prompt: What must be checked after malloc?
options: Whether the returned pointer is NULL
Whether the new value is positive
Whether the list is sorted
Whether the next node is larger
questions.answer: Whether the returned pointer is NULL
questions.explanation: malloc can fail. The program must not dereference a null result.

questions.prompt: When deleting a node, what is the safe order?
options: Reconnect the previous link, then free the removed node
Free the node, then read its next pointer
Set head to NULL in every case
Free the next node first
questions.answer: Reconnect the previous link, then free the removed node
questions.explanation: The list must retain a valid path to remaining nodes, and the removed node must not be accessed after free.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of searching an unsorted singly linked list of n nodes?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: In the worst case the search examines every node because nodes are reached sequentially.
